source: Murphy et al. (2008) Debugging: the good, the bad, and the quirky - a qualitative analysis of novices' strategies
finding: Founding qualitative study of how novice (CS) students debug. It sorted strategies into good, bad and quirky ones. Full text was paywalled and not read; only the Semantic Scholar record (152 citations, no abstract, no open PDF) was seen.
numbers: Not verified: sample size and strategy counts. Record shows 152 citations.
limits: Closed access. Treat any detail beyond the title as unverified. Needs a later pass via a library copy.
agent_relevance: Anchor for the claim that novice debugging is a set of identifiable strategies, some of them harmful. A scaffold should name and block the bad ones (random edits, guess-and-check).

source: McCauley et al. (2008) Debugging: a review of the literature from an educational perspective
finding: Main review of debugging in computing education. Full text closed. Metadata only seen: 284 citations.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Closed access.
agent_relevance: Use as the entry point for backward citation tracing, not as a source of numbers yet.

source: Fitzgerald et al. (2008) Debugging: finding, fixing and flailing, a multi-institutional study of novice debuggers
finding: Multi-institutional study of novice debuggers. As reported by Kurniawan et al. (2025): once students find and locate a bug, they are generally able to fix it. So the hard part is finding, not fixing. Full text closed; 235 citations per Semantic Scholar.
numbers: Not verified directly; the claim is second-hand via Kurniawan et al. (evidence line a12).
limits: Second-hand claim. Study sample not seen.
agent_relevance: Supports putting effort into localisation (hypothesis, trace, narrowing) rather than into repair generation. Matches the shape of the schema: locate first.

source: Qian & Lehman (2017) Students' misconceptions and other difficulties in introductory programming: a literature review
finding: Standard review of novice misconceptions in intro programming. Bronze open-access link blocked by the ACM site (returned an HTML wall, not a PDF), so not read. 635 citations.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Source for the taxonomy of misconceptions (syntax, conceptual, strategic). Henley et al. cite it for the claim that novices struggle with program behaviour.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2026) Reasoning Trajectories for Socratic Debugging of Student Code
finding: Frames novice bugs as caused by misconceptions (false beliefs). Defines a Reasoning Trajectory (RT): deductive steps from the failed test to a statement that contradicts the misconception. A Socratic conversation is then built with one teacher turn per RT step. Dataset: 227 (problem, buggy solution, misconception) triplets, over 22K RT steps, 14 LLM configurations.
numbers: Best RT validity about 91.1% (GPT-5 medium effort, 1,271 steps). GPT-5 low effort conversation validity 98.7%, turn grounding 99.4%. Claude Haiku-4.5 without reasoning had 62.6% RT validity with the most steps (1,962). Reasoning mode: Sonnet-4.5 +6.6 points RT validity, Haiku-4.5 +16.3, GPT-5 -0.8 for one setting.
quote: In Socratic debugging, instructors guide students towards identifying and fixing a bug on their own.
limits: Judge is an LLM (Claude Sonnet-4.5 thinking). Agreement with one human expert on 30 RTs was only 76.7%; on 88 teacher turns 96.6%. Static conversations, no real students. Longer RT means more chances for one invalid step.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a belief-contradiction operator: derive a consequence that conflicts with the held belief, do not hand over the fix. Also shows longer chains lower validity, so keep chains short and checked.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2026) RT prompt design (same paper, Section 4)
finding: The RT prompt has five rules: strictly deductive steps, stay consistent with the student's false belief, aim only to disprove the misconception, start from observable facts in the failed test, label steps and cite premises. 2-shot for RT, 1-shot for conversation.
numbers: Example: x + y / 2 with x=1,y=3 gives 2.5. RT lists both groupings, computes (1+3)/2=2.0, and shows it differs from 2.5.
limits: Success patterns named by the authors: exhaust the alternatives, trace with concrete values. Failure patterns less quantified.
agent_relevance: Good recipe for a hypothesis-elimination step: enumerate alternatives, compute each on concrete values, compare with the observation.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2026) Judge reliability (same paper, 5.2.2)
finding: An LLM judge was checked against a human on small subsets. Agreement was 76.7% on 30 RT samples (10 each from three models) and 96.6% on 88 Socratic turns. The expert penalised wrong terminology the judge missed.
numbers: 30 RTs, 88 turns.
limits: Tiny validation sets. Headline 91% validity inherits judge error.
agent_relevance: Warns that LLM-graded reasoning validity numbers are soft. Our scaffold evals of reasoning chains should use a second, independent check.

source: Yeltekin & Bauer (2026) Can LLMs Simulate Novice Programmers' Misconceptions?
finding: 13 LLMs tested on 30 Python misconceptions from ProgMiscon, with 60 generated code-tracing questions (MC and True/False). Four tasks: solve, solve open-ended, simulate a student holding the misconception, diagnose the misconception.
numbers: Solve MC/TF: Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.6 variants 100%; Qwen2.5:7b 83.3%. Open-ended (n=27): top models 96-100%, Qwen2.5:7b 63.0%. Simulation 'followed misconception': Opus 5 96.7%, GPT-5.6 Sol 95.0%, Sonnet 5 90.0%, Qwen3-coder:30b 45.0%, Qwen2.5:7b 38.3% (it answered correctly 55.0%).
quote: Code-tuned models fail during misconception simulation by reverting to correct execution.
limits: Short paper. Only 30 misconceptions, generated questions, only 27 questions solvable without options. LLM-matched answers with human review.
agent_relevance: Code-tuned models revert to correct execution when asked to hold a false belief. So an agent cannot easily 'play the novice' to model a user's bug; and it may silently correct a wrong premise.

source: Yeltekin & Bauer (2026) Misconception diagnosis (same paper, Table 3)
finding: Given a question and the misconception answer, models name the misconception. Free-text diagnosis is harder than picking from the list of 30. True/False items are easier than multiple-choice.
numbers: Free text (Exp 4): GPT-5.6 Sol 91.7%, Sonnet 5 88.3%, Opus 5 86.7%, Qwen2.5:7b 55.0%. From list (Exp 5): GPT-5.6 Sol 98.3%, Opus 5 96.7%, Qwen2.5:7b 53.3%. MC vs TF in free text: Opus 76.7% vs 96.7%.
limits: Closed list of 30 makes the list task easy. Not real student answers; the wrong answer is designed to match.
agent_relevance: Diagnosing the false belief from a single wrong output works for large models when candidates are listed. Offering a candidate list is a cheap scaffold.

source: Henley et al. (2021) An Inquisitive Code Editor for Addressing Novice Programmers' Misconceptions of Program Behavior
finding: Tool concept: the editor asks the novice questions about program behaviour that static analysis can check. A wrong answer triggers an explanation plus inserted assertions and comments. Three goals: identify, correct, prevent misconceptions. Contrasts with Whyline, which needs the user to already know a bug exists.
numbers: Cites: Whyline users fixed bugs in half the time of a traditional debugger; students took substantially longer to fix semantic errors than syntax errors. No new experiment; prototype for Atom plus informal surveys.
quote: The code editor asks questions about program behavior that can be validated with static analysis.
limits: Concept paper. Claims about prior studies are second-hand. No learning-outcome data.
agent_relevance: A 'predict then check' probe: ask for the expected behaviour before running, compare with actual. Surfaces false beliefs early. Fits a prediction-check operator.

source: Kurniawan et al. (2025) Designing for Novice Debuggers: A Pilot Study on an AI-Assisted Debugging Tool (CodeHinter)
finding: CodeHinter combines spectrum-based fault localisation with LLM hints and quizzes, so students stay engaged instead of receiving the fix. Ten undergraduates, 50 minutes, two tasks each, crossover vs earlier tool SID. Localising the faulty line was the most valued feature.
numbers: N=10 (8 first-year, 2 second-year). SUS 75/100 vs 65/100 for SID. Satisfaction 89/100 vs 60/100. Locate-line feature rated 4.5/5. 'End-to-End Test' helpful for all 10 (8 strongly agree). 6 of 10 still clicked 'Provide Code Solution'. Only 2 regularly used debugging tools; 5 had never heard of any.
limits: Tiny N, self-report only, no learning measure, no control for time. Authors say they need profile-based personalisation.
agent_relevance: Even with a hint-first design, 6 of 10 novices went for the solution. Guardrails need enforcement, not only offering. Localisation is the valued step.

source: Kurniawan et al. (2025) Related-work claims (same paper)
finding: Summarises: novices struggle with error messages; LLM tools resolve some semantic errors but accuracy varies; fixes may differ a lot from student code; LLMs may add new errors novices cannot spot. Cites Leinonen et al.: Codex explanations were helpful but suggested fixes were correct only 33% of the time. Cites Fitzgerald et al.: once bugs are located, students generally fix them.
numbers: Codex fix correct 33% (second-hand). PyDex repair rate 96.5% (second-hand).
limits: All second-hand figures from other papers.
agent_relevance: Backs the design rule: show where and why, keep edits small, check the fix.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Generative AI for Programming Education: Benchmarking ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Human Tutors
finding: Six scenarios; this line covers repair and hints. Five Python problems with real buggy student programs, 25 instances per method, two human experts as evaluators. GPT-4 near tutors on repair, far below on hints.
numbers: Repair correct: ChatGPT 68.0%, GPT-4 88.0%, Tutor 100.0%. Edit tokens: GPT-4 36.6 vs Tutor 19.0. Hint 'Overall' good quality: ChatGPT 18.0%, GPT-4 66.0%, Tutor 92.0%. Hint conceal: ChatGPT 38.0, GPT-4 72.0, Tutor 94.0. Hint correct: GPT-4 74.0.
limits: 25 instances only, single query per LLM, models now old (2023), only two evaluators who are also the tutors.
agent_relevance: GPT-4 makes larger edits than tutors; ChatGPT often reveals the answer in a hint. A minimal-edit and a do-not-reveal check are separable and measurable.

source: Phung et al. (2023) PyFiXV: High-Precision Feedback for Programming Syntax Errors
finding: Codex generates a fix plus explanation; a run-time validation step decides whether to show it. Gives educators a precision knob. Tested on TigerJython and Codeforces syntax-error data, 240 buggy programs each, three expert annotators.
numbers: Baseline PyFi-PEM precision 5.0 (TigerJython, Python 2) and 35.0 (Codeforces). PyFiXV at P70 coverage 64.2 on Codeforces. Split: 25% test, 50% few-shot, 25% calibration.
limits: Syntax errors only (the authors say semantic errors are future work). Codex is retired. Newer Python messages raise the baseline.
agent_relevance: Validate-before-showing with a tunable precision threshold is a transferable guardrail: abstain when unsure.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Studying the effect of AI Code Generators on Supporting Novice Learners in Introductory Programming
finding: Controlled experiment, 69 novices aged 10-17, 10 sessions, 45 Python authoring tasks each followed by a modification task. Half had Codex. Codex raised authoring performance without hurting later manual modification. Retention a week later was not significantly better.
numbers: Training completion Codex 90.9% vs Baseline 79.0% (t(67)=2.8, p=.006, d=0.68). Authoring correctness 80.1% vs 44.4% (d=1.67). Time 210s vs 361s. Errors per task 1.28 vs 2.17 (d=0.74); syntax errors 0.87 vs 1.67. Retention authoring 59.1% vs 49.8% (p=.262); modifying 47.5% vs 34.8% (p=.092).
limits: Only novices with no prior text-based coding; ages 10-17; Python after Scratch. Retention effect not significant. Codex group had more errors on retention authoring (1.58 vs 0.99, p=.042).
agent_relevance: Assistance lifts task success but learning evidence is weak. For our agent as a helper, tasks pass but the human's skill transfer is unproven.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) High vs low prior skill split (same paper)
finding: Benefit depended on prior knowledge. Learners with higher Scratch pre-test who had Codex did significantly better on retention than matched baseline; low pre-test learners showed near-identical results.
numbers: Pre-test knowledge Codex 62.7% vs Baseline 60% (p=.67). Codex not used for 26.5% of tasks. 32% of prompts (530 of 1,646) were identical to the task text.
limits: Subgroup split after the fact; exact subgroup N not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding helps those with a base. A debugging scaffold may help strong users more than weak ones, an expertise-reversal pattern.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Exploring the Responses of LLMs to Beginner Programmers' Help Requests
finding: 150 real help requests from an online programming course, 275 issues found by annotators (1.9 per request). Codex and GPT-3.5 asked to find and explain issues. GPT-3.5 often finds one real issue but not all and often invents issues.
numbers: Issue themes: logic errors 72% of requests, input/output 34%, syntax 8.0%, very incomplete 5.3%. GPT-3.5 (English): at least one real issue 90%; all issues 57%; non-existent issues 40%; included code 100%; model solution 67%. Codex English: 70% / 13% / 40% / 33% code.
quote: GPT-3.5 in 90% of the cases ... False positives are common (40% chance for GPT-3.5).
limits: Models are old (2023). Single course. Subset of 120 responses used for the model comparison.
agent_relevance: LLMs make the same mistakes as novices (false positives) and ignore 'do not give code'. Output filtering is needed.

source: Hellas et al. (2023) Logic-error finding and instruction-following (same paper)
finding: Instructed not to provide sample code or tests, GPT-3.5 practically always included code, often a model solution. Responses were pedagogically unsuitable on the six very incomplete programs.
numbers: In the best-case exercise all issues were addressed in 10 of 10 responses; worst case 1 of 10. Even the best case had 4 of 10 with false positives.
limits: Qualitative sample.
agent_relevance: Do-not-reveal instructions alone fail. Needs a verifier that rejects answers containing the solution.

source: Liffiton et al. (2023) CodeHelp: Using LLMs with Guardrails for Scalable Support in Programming Classes
finding: Deployed tool that refuses to reveal solutions, using a pipeline of prompts. 52 students, 12-week course, 49 analysed. Each query is one-shot with no dialogue, to limit LLM drift. Students valued availability and help with error messages.
numbers: About half the class used it each week; roughly 70% in four or more weeks; roughly 80% sent 10 or more queries; about 50% sent 30 or more; 7 of 49 over 100 queries, one over 600. 45 completed the survey. Cost about $0.002 per query.
limits: Single course, GPT-3.5 era, self-selected use, no learning outcome test.
agent_relevance: Guardrail design from real deployment: one-shot, hint-not-solution, cheap. Shows heavy use by a few: over-reliance risk concentrates.

source: Leinonen et al. (2023) Comparing Code Explanations Created by Students and LLMs
finding: About 1000 students wrote explanations (954 in Lab A); GPT-3 explanations of three functions were rated by students on 5-point scales. LLM explanations were rated easier and more accurate than student ones.
numbers: Easy to understand: students 3.75 vs LLM 4.12 (medians 4.0). Accurate summary: 3.78 vs 4.0. Each rater saw 54 explanations of mixed sources.
limits: Perception ratings by novices, not expert accuracy; three functions only; GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Novices can be convinced by fluent explanations. Perceived accuracy is not correctness, a risk when the agent explains bugs to users.

source: Henley et al. (2021) Cited evidence on novices' view of correctness (same paper)
finding: Novices often hold a different definition of program correctness than experts. One cited study found many students believe a program is correct when there are no compiler errors. Enhanced compiler error messages gave inconsistent or inconclusive results across six cited studies.
numbers: No new numbers. References [34], [50], [1] in that paper.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: 'No error' is not 'correct': the agent should check behaviour against intent, not only for crashes.

source: Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2026) Misconception as root cause and dissonance mechanism
finding: Theory frame: most novice bugs come from misconceptions, i.e. false beliefs. A direct contradiction between belief and observed behaviour should create cognitive dissonance that makes the learner update the belief and keep the update. Cites zone of proximal development, Socratic scaffolding, repeated retrieval.
numbers: No measured learning effect in this paper; only generation validity.
quote: Placing learners in a state of cognitive dissonance is ideal for learning in problem-solving scenarios.
limits: The dissonance and durability claims are assumed, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Same loop for an agent: state the belief, derive a prediction, test it, update. The belief change comes from the contradiction.

source: Yeltekin & Bauer (2026) Model size and coder bias (same paper)
finding: Small and code-tuned models fail to hold a wrong belief; Qwen3-coder's reasoning chain starts as the misconception, then stops and solves the question correctly. Authors do not find systematic differences in solving between coder and non-coder models.
numbers: Followed misconception: Qwen3-coder:30b 45.0% vs Qwen3:30b 86.7%; Qwen2.5-coder:14b 55.0% vs Qwen2.5:14b 61.7%; Qwen2.5-coder:7b 53.4% vs Qwen2.5:7b 38.3%. So the coder penalty shows in Qwen3 but not in all pairs.
limits: Mixed pairs; small N (60 items); local models via Ollama.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a coding-tuned model can reason under a user's false premise. Use large reasoning models for belief simulation.

source: Phung et al. (2023) Solving check and tutor gap (benchmark paper)
finding: Before the education scenarios, GPT-4 solved all five problems and ChatGPT solved four of five (failed FIBONACCI repeatedly). The gap with tutors was worst on FIBONACCI for repair and on PALINDROME for hints.
numbers: GPT-4 5/5, ChatGPT 4/5 solved. Hint explanation correct: ChatGPT 40.0, GPT-4 70.0, Tutor 94.0.
limits: One query per LLM; 25 instances.
agent_relevance: Being able to solve the task does not mean being able to tutor it well. Check teaching output separately from solving.

source: Murphy et al. (2008) Position in the field (metadata only)
finding: Semantic Scholar shows 152 citations; the ACM page returned 403 and Unpaywall needs an email address, which we did not send. So the founding paper remains unread in this run.
numbers: 152 citations.
limits: No text. Flagged for a manual pass.
agent_relevance: Do not quote specific Murphy numbers from memory in later documents.

source: Kazemitabaar et al. (2023) Documentation use and errors (same paper)
finding: Learners with Codex opened the documentation much less on authoring tasks and made fewer syntax errors. Data-type errors were not different.
numbers: Docs access Codex 22.1% vs Baseline 54.3% (d=1.33). Syntax errors 0.87 vs 1.67 (d=0.88). Data-type errors 0.30 vs 0.39 (p=.331).
limits: Error counts came from shell logs.
agent_relevance: Help tools remove surface errors, not deeper type errors. Suggests where a scaffold adds value: semantics.
